lesson.title: Counting Atoms With Greek Prefixes
lesson.summary: Naming covalent compounds uses a system of Greek numerical prefixes attached to element names to specify exactly how many atoms of each element are present, distinguishing it sharply from the naming of ionic compounds.
lesson.body:
Covalent compounds form when two nonmetal elements share electrons rather than transferring them outright, and this creates a naming problem that ionic compounds do not have. In an ionic compound built from compounds and covalent bonds, charges balance in a predictable way, so a formula like MgCl2 can only mean one thing and the name magnesium chloride is unambiguous. Two nonmetals, however, can often combine in more than one ratio. Nitrogen and oxygen alone form at least NO, NO2, N2O, N2O3, N2O4, and N2O5, each a distinct, stable compound with different properties. Naming these correctly requires specifying the exact number of atoms of each element, which is exactly what the covalent naming system is built to do.

The system uses Greek numerical prefixes attached directly to each element's name: mono for one, di for two, tri for three, tetra for four, penta for five, hexa for six, hepta for seven, octa for eight, nona for nine, and deca for ten. The first element in the formula keeps its normal element name, and the prefix mono is conventionally omitted for that first element only, since a single atom of it is assumed by default. The second element always gets a prefix, including mono when there is only one atom of it, and its ending is changed to "ide," the same ending used for simple anions in ionic naming.

Applying this to the nitrogen oxides gives a clean, unambiguous set of names. NO is nitrogen monoxide, since there is one nitrogen, no prefix needed, and one oxygen, so mono is included on the second element. NO2 is nitrogen dioxide. N2O is dinitrogen monoxide, commonly known as laughing gas. N2O3 is dinitrogen trioxide. N2O4 is dinitrogen tetroxide, note that the "a" in tetra is dropped before the vowel in oxide for smoother pronunciation, a small spelling adjustment that also applies to penta before oxide in some compounds. N2O5 is dinitrogen pentoxide. Each name maps to exactly one formula, which is the entire point of the system.

A few additional conventions round out the rules. Carbon monoxide, CO, is one of the most familiar examples, correctly using mono on the second element despite it being commonly written without the prefix in casual speech; the formal name always includes it. Some compounds with well established common names, such as water for H2O and ammonia for NH3, are kept as exceptions rather than being renamed dihydrogen monoxide or nitrogen trihydride in everyday use, though the systematic names are still technically valid. When you encounter a covalent formula, count the atoms of each element, look up or recall the matching prefix, keep the first element's name plain unless it is exactly one atom needing no prefix at all, and change the second element's ending to ide. This prefix based approach is only used for compounds between two nonmetals; as soon as a metal is involved, the compound is very likely ionic, and the different naming rules for compounds and covalent bonds no longer apply.
